05:46 - Alligator 1

Instagram - http://instagram.com/barnydillarstone

_____________________________________________

RESOURCES:

- McClain et al. 2019, the original alligator fall experiment at ~2,000 m: isopods on the first carcass within 43 hours, the second stripped to bone by day 51, and the third gone after 8 days with the 45 lb harness and weight dragged 8 m (the large elasmobranch suggestion). Also the source for the deep-sea carbon-deficit motivation: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0225345 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6924670
- Bryant, Nunnally, Hanks & McClain 2022, the sediment study around the 19.5 kg alligator. It found up to three times more carbon than background sediment and argues that the size threshold for enriching sediments is lower than assumed: https://doi.org/10.1111/maec.12707
- Berman, Hiley, Read & Rouse 2024, the formal description of Osedax craigmcclaini from the alligator bones, and Osedax bozoi from cow bones at the same Gulf depth (Zootaxa 5443(3): 337–352): https://doi.org/10.11646/zootaxa.5443.3.2 and https://zenodo.org/record/11045291
- Danise & Higgs 2015, Osedax borings in ~100-million-year-old plesiosaur and sea turtle bones, showing the worms fed on marine reptile falls before whales existed: https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2015.0072 and https://pearl.plymouth.ac.uk/handle/10026.1/3329
- Smith, Glover, Treude, Higgs & Amon 2015, the whale-fall review covering successional stages, bone lipids and whale falls as evolutionary stepping stones: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-marine-010213-135144 and https://core.ac.uk/works/100908260
- McClain, Nunnally, Chapman & Barry 2018, the 5-year wood fall experiment at 3,203 m, where more wood meant more species: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10166878
- McClain & Barry 2014, wood fall community composition tracking energy availability: https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2014.0129
- Bienhold et al. 2013, how deep-sea wood falls sustain chemosynthetic life: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0053590
- Smith et al. 2016, the 27-year abyssal Pacific time series where sinking carbon met only about 63% of seafloor demand, for the carbon-deficit point: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7175715

Your biology protecting you from the billions of microorganisms that want to consume you and from your own perverted cells that turn into cancer. videos.title: Why this black hole photo is such a big deal
videos.description:
What it took to collect these 54-million-year-old photons from a supermassive black hole.

Become a Video Lab member! http://bit.ly/video-lab

This is an updated version of a video we published in 2016 about the Event Horizon Telescope, an international collaboration to image a black hole for the first time in human history. 

On April 10, 2019, the team announced their results: They had successfully imaged the supermassive black hole in the center of the galaxy m87, which is nearly 54 million light-years away from us. They were able to achieve unprecedented resolution using very long baseline interferometry, which combines the observations of multiple radio telescopes across the globe. 

The team wanted to find out whether Einstein's Theory of General Relativity holds up in the extreme environment of black holes, and the results do, in fact, seem to be consistent with the predictions. In the future, we may see more and shaper images of black holes as the team targets smaller wavelengths of light and recruits more telescopes. Eventually, they may include an orbiting space telescope.

videos.title: The eclipse photo that made Einstein famous
videos.description:
In 1919, a total solar eclipse helped redefine gravity.

Thanks to Raycon for sponsoring this video. Check them out at http://buyraycon.com/vox

Become a Video Lab member! http://bit.ly/video-lab

Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity, published in 1915, defined gravity as the influence of massive objects, like planets and stars, curving space around them. This was very different from the way Isaac Newton had defined gravity over 200 years earlier: Newton described an attracting force that kept planets and stars in orbit with each other. If Einstein was right, then light would also bend near massive objects. And in 1919, two British expeditions set out to test it by photographing a total solar eclipse. By comparing the position of stars with the sun in front of them and another with the sun elsewhere, Arthur Eddington and his team proved that the stars’ apparent positions moved during the eclipse. This was the first, but not the last time Einstein’s theory of general relativity was tested and proven, and Einstein became a celebrity overnight. He remained a pop culture icon for the rest of his life.
